Why we stopped billing by the hour and never looked back.

When we started Fernway Studio, we did what every agency does: we charged hourly. The result was that 4 of our first 6 projects went over budget. Clients were frustrated, we were frustrated, and trust was eroding.

So in 2024 we made a bold decision. We switched to a fixed price: KES 450,000 per Shopify store. Period.

It changed everything. Clients know exactly what they are paying. We are incentivized to work smarter, not longer. And our relationships are built on trust instead of timesheets.

Since then we have launched 31 stores, and only 2 went over our 6-week timeline.

Pricing isn't just a number. It's a promise.

Founders, how do you price your services? Let me know in the comments.

#Entrepreneurship #Africa #Shopify #AgencyLife #Pricing

When we launched Patchwork CI, we promised it would always be free for open source. Some people told us we were crazy and asked how we planned to make money.

Today we run on 1,200 repositories, and about 900 of them are open source.

One thing in the data surprised me. Across all of those repositories, 1 in 7 CI failures turned out to be a flaky test. That adds up to a lot of developer time spent on red builds that were not real failures.

Open source gave us more than users. It gave us data, feedback, and a community. Our most-requested feature, GitLab support, came straight from OSS maintainers, and we shipped it on November 12.

Giving back is not charity. It is strategy.

#OpenSource #DevOps #CI #DeveloperExperience #BuildInPublic

Losing our first big customer was the best thing that ever happened to Ledgerline.

They walked away 5 months in, and it stung. But failure is part of success, not its opposite.

The reason they left was that they had heavily customized their NetSuite instance, and we only supported standard fields. We were not meeting them where they were.

So we listened, we learned, and we built. We spent 6 weeks adding support for custom fields, and it changed how we think about our customers.

Today we serve 38 customers, and 11 of them rely on custom fields.

Your biggest setback can become your biggest breakthrough. Lean into the hard feedback. Your customers are telling you what to build, you just have to listen.

What's a loss that shaped your company?

#Startups #SaaS #Leadership #CustomerSuccess #Growth

Nobody used the app we built.

When we launched Rotaship, the mobile app looked great and we assumed restaurant staff would take to it. In the first month, only 12% of staff even opened it. That was the wake-up call. We hadn't solved the real problem; we had added to it.

Restaurant teams don't want another app. They already live on WhatsApp.

So in 2025 we made the hard decision to move everything there. It worked: 140 outlets now use it, and the median reply time to shift messages is under 20 minutes.

Meet your users where they already are instead of asking them to come to you. Sometimes the best product decision is giving up the thing you love.

#ProductManagement #Indonesia #StartupLessons #UserExperience

Hardware is hard, and our first production run at Shelfwise proved it.

We shipped 400 labels with a faulty battery contact. As a young hardware startup, it would have been easy to cut corners. Instead, we recalled and replaced all 400 labels at our own cost, which set us back about $7,000. It was painful, but it was the right call, because trust is everything.

We also introduced a 100% contact test at the factory. Since then, we have had zero contact failures across 6,000 labels.

Mistakes don't define you. How you respond to them does. Own your mistakes, fix them fast, and build systems so they never happen again.

#Hardware #Startups #Manufacturing #Leadership #Integrity

After 11 years in a clinic, I walked away. Here's why.

Years ago, I worked as a maintenance engineer at an auto-parts plant in Pune. One day a spindle failed, and the whole line was down for 3 days. We raised our prices by 50% and here's what happened.

In September we made one of the scariest decisions in Tabwise's history: going from $8 to $12 per user per month. Our support costs per customer had doubled since launch, so we had a choice to make. We could compromise on quality, or charge what the product is worth.

We chose to charge what it's worth.

Still, we didn't want to punish loyal customers, so anyone already with us kept the $8 price for 12 months.

The result? In the following 2 months, only 2 out of 140 customers churned. Two.

What I took away from this: customers are paying for outcomes, so price accordingly.
